subsections.subsection_title: 1. What the OSCE station may say

items.text: You are asked to take a focused history from a 24-year-old woman presenting with vaginal discharge.
A 28-year-old woman presents with offensive-smelling vaginal discharge. Take a history, give your differential diagnoses and outline management.
Examine a patient with vaginal discharge and explain your findings.
A vaginal swab reveals Candida albicans. Explain the result and manage the patient.
A woman presents with yellow-green discharge and dysuria following unprotected sexual intercourse. Assess and manage her.
A pregnant woman presents with vaginal discharge and vulval itching. Assess her and outline safe management.
A woman has recurrent vaginal discharge despite previous treatment. Explain your approach.

blocks.text: Examiner's priority: Can you identify the cause, assess STI risk without judgement, recognise red flags, and provide appropriate treatment and partner advice?
Start every consultation professionally.
Suggested opening statement

Good morning. My name is Dr. … I understand that you have been experiencing vaginal discharge. I would like to ask you some questions to understand the problem and determine what investigations or treatment you might need. Some questions will be about your menstrual and sexual health, which I routinely ask patients with this condition. The information you share will be treated confidentially, subject to the usual safety and legal exceptions. Is that alright with you?

items.text: Confirm the patient's name and age.
Ensure privacy and a comfortable environment.
Ask permission before discussing sensitive sexual history.
Use neutral, non-judgemental language.
Explain that an intimate examination may be needed, obtain separate consent, offer a chaperone, and allow the patient to stop the examination at any time.
Ask about pain before examining the abdomen or performing a pelvic examination.

blocks.text: Important: Do not assume that vaginal discharge means an STI or infidelity. Normal physiological discharge is common, and infections can occur without recent sexual exposure.
Use the following structured approach during the OSCE.

content_groups.group_title: A. Presenting complaint and history of presenting complaint

blocks.text: Ask about the discharge in detail.

blocks.text: Clarify whether the discharge is different from the patient's usual discharge and whether it is associated with menstruation, intercourse, pregnancy or use of a new product.

content_groups.group_title: B. Associated symptoms and red flags

items.text: Fever, rigors or feeling systemically unwell.
Lower abdominal pain, deep dyspareunia or cervical motion pain if previously assessed.
Nausea or vomiting.
Abnormal vaginal bleeding.
Genital ulcers, blisters, rash or vulval swelling.
Urinary frequency, urgency or haematuria.
Missed period or possible pregnancy.
Recent childbirth, miscarriage, abortion or gynaecological procedure.
A retained tampon or other possible vaginal foreign body, where relevant.

blocks.text: Red flags requiring urgent assessment: severe pelvic pain, fever with pelvic symptoms, pregnancy with pain or bleeding, heavy bleeding, collapse, or suspected sepsis. Do not delay emergency care while waiting for swab results.

items.text: Date of the last menstrual period (LMP).
Whether periods are regular.
Whether there is intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding.
Whether pregnancy is possible.
Previous pregnancies and their outcomes.
Current pregnancy or recent delivery, if applicable.
Contraception used and any recent changes.

blocks.text: Pregnancy status affects both the differential diagnosis and the choice of medication.
Introduce this section sensitively and explain why it matters.

items.text: Are you currently sexually active?
Do you have sex with men, women or partners of more than one gender, where relevant to clinical assessment?
Have you had a new sexual partner recently?
Do you or your partner have other sexual partners?
Do you use condoms or other barrier protection?
Have you or your partner previously been diagnosed with an STI?
Have you noticed symptoms in your partner?
Have you previously been tested for HIV, syphilis, chlamydia or gonorrhoea?

blocks.text: Do not assume the patient's relationship status, sexual practices or STI risk. Ask only what is clinically relevant and respect confidentiality.

content_groups.group_title: E. Previous treatment and medical history

items.text: Previous diagnoses of candidiasis, BV, trichomoniasis or cervicitis.
Previous antibiotics, antifungals or over-the-counter vaginal preparations.
Diabetes, immunosuppression or HIV, when relevant.
Recent antibiotic use.
Drug allergies.
Regular medications.
Douching, perfumed soaps, vaginal washes or other irritants.
Previous pelvic surgery or gynaecological procedures.

blocks.text: Recurrent symptoms may reflect an incorrect initial diagnosis, mixed infection, reinfection, resistance, an underlying condition or non-infectious irritation.
The main diagnoses you should know are physiological discharge, bacterial vaginosis, vulvovaginal candidiasis, trichomoniasis and cervicitis.
1. Physiological vaginal discharge

items.text: Clear or white, usually non-offensive.
No significant itching, soreness or pelvic pain.
Varies with ovulation, pregnancy and hormonal contraception.
Examination usually shows no inflammation.

blocks.text: Clue: Normal discharge without associated symptoms.
2. Bacterial vaginosis (BV)

items.text: Thin, homogeneous grey-white discharge.
Fishy odour, sometimes more noticeable after intercourse or menstruation.
Usually little vulval inflammation or itching.
Vaginal pH is typically above 4.5.

blocks.text: Clue: Fishy smell + thin discharge + pH above 4.5.
3. Vulvovaginal candidiasis

items.text: Thick, white, curd-like discharge may occur.
Marked itching, soreness, redness or swelling.
External dysuria may occur when urine touches inflamed skin.
Vaginal pH is usually normal, at or below 4.5.

blocks.text: Clue: Intense itching + vulval inflammation + normal pH.
4. Trichomoniasis

items.text: May cause yellow-green, sometimes frothy discharge.
Offensive smell, itching or dysuria may occur.
Vaginal pH is commonly above 4.5.
Cervical punctate haemorrhages, sometimes called a strawberry cervix, may be seen but are not always present.

blocks.text: Clue: Frothy discharge with inflammation and possible STI exposure.
5. Cervicitis due to chlamydia or gonorrhoea

items.text: Mucopurulent discharge from the cervix.
Contact bleeding or postcoital bleeding.
Dysuria or pelvic discomfort may occur.
Many patients have few or no symptoms.

blocks.text: Clue: Mucopurulent cervical discharge, contact bleeding or STI risk.

items.text: Retained foreign body: persistent, often very offensive discharge, sometimes blood-stained.
Irritant or allergic vulvovaginitis: burning, itching or redness after soaps, antiseptics or vaginal products.
Genitourinary syndrome of menopause: dryness, irritation, painful intercourse and sometimes watery or yellowish discharge.
Pelvic inflammatory disease: discharge with pelvic pain, deep dyspareunia, cervical motion tenderness or fever.
Cervical or vaginal malignancy: persistent watery, blood-stained or offensive discharge, especially with postcoital or postmenopausal bleeding.

blocks.text: Discharge appearance is suggestive, not diagnostic. Mixed infections occur, and the classic descriptions are not always present.
In a practical OSCE, the examiner may ask you to describe or demonstrate the examination.

items.text: Assess whether the patient appears well or unwell.
Record temperature, pulse, blood pressure and respiratory rate as indicated.
Look for pallor if there is associated bleeding.
Assess hydration and signs of systemic illness where appropriate.

blocks.title: With consent, privacy and appropriate exposure:

items.text: Inspect the abdomen for distension or scars.
Palpate gently for tenderness, guarding or rebound tenderness.
Assess for suprapubic tenderness.
Look for a palpable mass if clinically indicated.

blocks.text: Pelvic tenderness, guarding or systemic illness should increase concern for PID or another acute abdominal or pelvic condition.
Explain the procedure, obtain consent, offer a chaperone and position the patient appropriately.

blocks.title: Inspect the vulva, perineum and surrounding skin for:

items.text: Erythema, swelling and excoriations.
Ulcers, vesicles or other lesions.
Fissures or skin changes.
Visible discharge at the vaginal introitus.
Signs of trauma or a foreign body, where visible.
Atrophy or other abnormalities.

blocks.text: A speculum examination may be indicated to assess the vaginal walls and cervix, identify the source of discharge and collect appropriate samples.

items.text: Explain the procedure and obtain informed consent.
Offer a chaperone and ensure privacy.
Position the patient comfortably in the dorsal lithotomy position, if appropriate.
Choose an appropriate-sized speculum and warm it with water; use lubricant compatible with planned testing when needed.
Gently insert the closed speculum, directing it posteriorly, and open it once appropriately positioned.
Inspect the vaginal walls for discharge, inflammation, lesions or a foreign body.
Visualise the cervix and assess for mucopurulent discharge, friability, contact bleeding or visible lesions.
Collect vaginal or cervical samples according to the tests required and local protocol.
Gently remove the speculum, check the patient's comfort and thank them.

blocks.text: Important: A bimanual examination is not mandatory for every uncomplicated vaginal discharge presentation. Perform it when indicated, particularly if pelvic pain, PID or a pelvic mass is suspected. Avoid delaying urgent treatment in a seriously unwell patient for a routine examination.
Choose investigations based on symptoms, examination findings, pregnancy status and STI risk. Not every patient needs every test.

blocks.text: Normal pH
Physiological discharge or candidiasis is more likely, depending on the symptoms and examination.
Raised pH
Supports BV or trichomoniasis, but can also occur with blood, semen, menopause-related changes and other conditions.
**B. Classic microscopy findings**

items.text: BV: clue cells, reduced lactobacilli and a positive amine test; Amsel criteria or Gram-stain scoring may be used.
Candidiasis: budding yeast, hyphae or pseudohyphae on microscopy, although microscopy can be negative.
Trichomoniasis: motile flagellated organisms on a fresh wet mount; a negative wet mount does not exclude infection.
Cervicitis: mucopurulent cervical discharge or cervical friability; NAAT helps identify chlamydia or gonorrhoea.

blocks.text: For BV, three of four Amsel criteria support the diagnosis: homogeneous discharge, pH above 4.5, positive amine test and clue cells. Where available, appropriate molecular tests or laboratory methods can improve diagnostic accuracy.
Management should be cause-specific. Avoid prescribing antibiotics or antifungals solely because discharge is present.

items.text: Reassure the patient.
Explain normal variation throughout the menstrual cycle and pregnancy.
Advise avoiding vaginal douching and perfumed products.
No antimicrobial treatment is required.

blocks.title: For symptomatic, confirmed or clinically diagnosed BV, commonly used first-line regimens include:

items.text: Metronidazole 400–500 mg orally twice daily for 7 days, according to local guidance; or
Metronidazole 0.75% vaginal gel, typically 5 g daily for 5 days, where available; or
Intravaginal clindamycin as an appropriate alternative.

blocks.text: Check pregnancy status, allergies, drug interactions and local protocols before prescribing. Routine treatment of male partners is not generally recommended under many established guidelines, although guidance is evolving and recurrent BV warrants review of current recommendations.

blocks.title: For uncomplicated candidiasis in a non-pregnant patient, options include:

items.text: A topical azole, such as clotrimazole, using an appropriate regimen; or
A single oral dose of fluconazole 150 mg, if suitable and pregnancy has been excluded.

blocks.text: In pregnancy: use a topical azole for 7 days. Avoid oral fluconazole during pregnancy.

For recurrent, severe or treatment-resistant candidiasis, confirm the diagnosis and consider culture or speciation. Review contributing factors, including diabetes and immunosuppression, and use a longer or specialist-directed regimen when indicated.

items.text: Treat with metronidazole, commonly 400–500 mg orally twice daily for 7 days in women.
Treat current sexual partners and advise avoiding sexual intercourse until both the patient and partners have completed treatment and symptoms have resolved.
Test for other STIs as appropriate.
Arrange retesting according to local guidance; women are commonly retested at approximately 3 months because reinfection is frequent.

content_groups.group_title: E. Cervicitis due to chlamydia or gonorrhoea

items.text: Collect appropriate NAAT samples.
Treat according to the organism, pregnancy status, local antimicrobial resistance patterns and current STI guidelines.
For chlamydia, doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days is a common regimen in non-pregnant adults; pregnancy requires an alternative, commonly azithromycin under local guidance.
Gonorrhoea requires an appropriate ceftriaxone-based regimen under current local guidance. Do not assume that a chlamydia regimen will adequately treat gonorrhoea.
Arrange partner notification and treatment, STI screening, and follow-up as indicated.

blocks.text: If cervicitis is strongly suspected and the patient is at high risk, has unreliable follow-up or cannot readily access testing, empirical treatment may be appropriate under local protocols.

If discharge is accompanied by pelvic pain and cervical motion, uterine or adnexal tenderness, consider PID. Start empiric broad-spectrum treatment promptly when clinically indicated, after appropriate assessment and sample collection where feasible.

Hospital assessment is indicated when there is severe illness, pregnancy, suspected tubo-ovarian abscess, inability to tolerate outpatient therapy, inability to exclude a surgical emergency, or failure to improve. Do not delay urgent treatment for laboratory confirmation.

content_groups.group_title: G. Foreign body, irritation or other causes

items.text: Remove a retained vaginal foreign body safely and assess for complications.
Stop irritant products and manage vulval inflammation appropriately.
Investigate persistent or unexplained blood-stained discharge, postcoital bleeding or postmenopausal bleeding.
Refer suspected malignancy urgently through the appropriate pathway.

subsections.subsection_title: 8. How to report your findings in the OSCE

blocks.text: The examiner wants a concise, organised clinical summary, followed by your likely diagnosis and plan.

“On examination, there is a thin, homogeneous grey-white vaginal discharge with a characteristic fishy odour. There is no marked vulval erythema or swelling. The vaginal pH is above 4.5, and microscopy demonstrates clue cells. These findings are consistent with bacterial vaginosis. I would assess for relevant STI risk, offer appropriate testing where indicated, and treat the symptomatic patient with a recommended metronidazole regimen.”

“There is thick, white, curd-like vaginal discharge with vulval erythema and excoriation. The patient reports significant vulval itching and soreness. Vaginal pH is within the normal acidic range, and microscopy demonstrates yeast forms. The findings are consistent with vulvovaginal candidiasis. I would assess pregnancy status, prescribe an appropriate antifungal, and investigate contributing factors if the condition is recurrent.”

“Speculum examination reveals mucopurulent discharge arising from the cervical os, with cervical friability and contact bleeding. These findings suggest cervicitis, with chlamydia and gonorrhoea among the differential diagnoses. I would obtain appropriate NAAT samples, assess for PID, offer relevant STI screening, and arrange treatment and partner management according to the findings and local guidelines.”

“There is clear-to-white, non-offensive discharge without vulval inflammation, ulceration or visible cervical abnormality. The patient has no associated itching, pelvic pain or abnormal bleeding. The findings are consistent with physiological vaginal discharge, although further testing would be guided by any persisting symptoms or relevant risk factors.”

“The patient has abnormal vaginal discharge associated with lower abdominal pain, cervical motion tenderness and fever. These findings raise concern for pelvic inflammatory disease. I would assess the patient's haemodynamic stability, pregnancy status and severity of illness, obtain appropriate samples without delaying treatment, initiate empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics and determine whether hospital admission is necessary.”

subsections.subsection_title: 9. Common examiner questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. What are the common causes of vaginal discharge?
Answer: Physiological discharge, BV, vulvovaginal candidiasis, trichomoniasis, cervicitis due to chlamydia or gonorrhoea, irritant vulvovaginitis and retained foreign bodies.
Q2. How do you differentiate BV from candidiasis?

Answer: BV typically causes thin, homogeneous, fishy-smelling discharge with pH above 4.5 and relatively little inflammation. Candidiasis typically causes intense itching, vulval erythema and thick discharge, with pH usually at or below 4.5.
Q3. What is a strawberry cervix?
Answer: A cervix with punctate red spots or petechiae, classically associated with trichomoniasis. It is not sufficiently sensitive to exclude infection when absent.
Q4. What is the difference between a low vaginal swab and an endocervical swab?

Answer: A low vaginal swab samples vaginal secretions and is useful for appropriate vaginal infection testing. An endocervical swab samples the cervical canal. For chlamydia and gonorrhoea, vaginal swabs or urine can be used for NAAT, depending on the assay and local protocol; an endocervical sample is not always necessary.
Q5. Does every woman with vaginal discharge need antibiotics?
Answer: No. Physiological discharge requires reassurance rather than antimicrobial treatment. Treatment should be guided by the likely cause, clinical findings and appropriate investigations.
Q6. What are the complications of untreated STIs causing discharge?

Answer: Depending on the organism, complications include PID, chronic pelvic pain, tubal infertility, ectopic pregnancy and transmission to sexual partners. Gonorrhoea can also cause disseminated infection, and some infections can affect pregnancy or the newborn.
Q7. How do you manage a pregnant woman with vaginal discharge?

Answer: Assess for physiological discharge, infection, membrane rupture if the history suggests fluid leakage, and obstetric complications. Investigate and treat confirmed or strongly suspected infections with pregnancy-appropriate regimens. Avoid oral fluconazole for candidiasis in pregnancy.
Q8. When would you admit a patient with vaginal discharge?

Answer: Admission is not required for uncomplicated discharge alone. It may be necessary for suspected severe PID, sepsis, pregnancy with significant pelvic symptoms, a suspected tubo-ovarian abscess, inability to tolerate outpatient treatment, or a possible surgical emergency.

items.text: Diagnosing an STI from the colour or smell of discharge alone.
Forgetting to ask about pregnancy and the last menstrual period.
Failing to ask about pelvic pain, fever or abnormal bleeding.
Omitting a confidential, non-judgemental sexual history.
Performing an intimate examination without consent or offering a chaperone.
Prescribing oral fluconazole to a pregnant patient.
Forgetting partner management for trichomoniasis and relevant bacterial STIs.
Treating every case with metronidazole without considering candidiasis or physiological discharge.
Failing to recognise PID or another urgent cause of pelvic pain.
Not arranging follow-up for persistent, recurrent or unexplained symptoms.
